title: South America
description: Irrigation, altitude and the Andes: Chile, Argentina and their neighbours.
L: Between the Andes and the Pacific
Explain the role of irrigation and the Andes

Chile is about 4,300 km long but rarely more than 180 km wide, between the Andes and the Pacific. Its isolation, protected by the Atacama desert in the north, the mountains, the ocean and Antarctic ice, has kept phylloxera out, so most vines grow on their own roots. The Central Valley holds most vineyards.

The Central Valley has a Mediterranean climate, with dry summers. Rivers fed by Andean snowmelt provide irrigation. Cold air flowing down from the mountains at night gives a wide day and night swing. Maipo, near Santiago, is Chile's historic Cabernet region; Colchagua and Cachapoal, in the Rapel Valley, make ripe reds.
Why are most Chilean vines grown on their own roots?
Natural barriers have kept phylloxera out, so grafting isn't needed.

Carmenère came from Bordeaux in the 19th century and was mixed up with Merlot. In 1994 it was identified, and it became Chile's signature grape. It needs a long, warm season; when ripe it gives dark fruit, spice and soft tannin; when unripe, a strong green pepper note.
Match each Chilean valley to its focus.
Chile's valleys differ by distance from the sea and the Andes.
Chile is long, narrow and free of phylloxera
Andean snowmelt irrigates the dry Central Valley
Carmenère, identified in 1994, is Chile's signature grape
Explain the influence of the Humboldt Current

The cold Humboldt Current runs north along Chile's coast, cooling the air and bringing morning fog. Coastal valleys like Casablanca, San Antonio and Leyda are among Chile's coolest, ideal for Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. This east to west contrast matters more than north to south.

In 2011 Chile added three descriptors to its regions: Costa, for coastal areas; Entre Cordilleras, between the mountain ranges; and Andes, for the foothills. A Costa wine is likely to be fresh and lower in alcohol; an Andes wine to have firm tannin and freshness from altitude.
In Chile, distance from the coast often matters more than latitude for climate.
Yes. The cold Humboldt Current cools coastal areas, while inland valleys get warmer before the Andes cool them again.

In the north, Limarí and Elqui have limestone soils and coastal fog, making mineral Chardonnay and Syrah. In the south, Itata, Bío-Bío and Malleco are cooler and wetter, with old dry-farmed vines of País and Cinsault, and new plantings of Riesling and Pinot Noir.
Limarí in the north; Itata in the south
Which Chilean region is best known for cool, coastal Sauvignon Blanc?
Casablanca's coastal location brings fog and cool air, perfect for crisp whites.
The Humboldt Current cools Chile's coast
Costa, Entre Cordilleras and Andes describe position
Limarí and Itata extend Chile north and south
A desert at the foot of the Andes

Mendoza produces about 70% of Argentina's wine. It is a high desert with under 250 mm of rain a year, sitting in the Andes' rain shadow. Irrigation comes from rivers fed by snowmelt, historically through channels built by the Huarpe people and later the Spanish. Hail is a constant threat; nets protect many vineyards.

Mendoza's vineyards lie from about 700 to 1,500 m. Higher sites have cooler nights, preserving acidity, and stronger ultraviolet light, which thickens skins for more colour and tannin. That's why Malbec there is dark and ripe yet fresh. The Zonda, a hot, dry wind, can harm flowering in spring.
What protects many Mendoza vineyards from a frequent hazard?
Summer hailstorms are common in Mendoza; nets shield the grapes.

Luján de Cuyo, south of Mendoza city, was the first DOC in Argentina, in 1989, known for old-vine Malbec. Maipú is nearby and historic. The Valle de Uco, at 900 to 1,500 m, has Argentina's most acclaimed new sites, like Gualtallary, Paraje Altamira and Los Chacayes, now recognised as geographical indications.
Luján de Cuyo and the Valle de Uco
Match each Mendoza area to its feature.
Mendoza's quality grows with altitude and site detail.
Mendoza is a high, irrigated desert making 70% of Argentina's wine
Altitude gives cool nights and strong light
Luján de Cuyo and the Valle de Uco are key sub-regions
Name San Juan and other regions

In the far north, Salta's Calchaquí Valleys hold some of the world's highest vineyards, from 1,700 to over 3,000 m. Cafayate is the centre. Torrontés, a cross of Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica, gives floral, aromatic whites. Malbec and Cabernet there are dark and intense, thanks to strong sun and cold nights.

In the south, Patagonia's Neuquén and Río Negro are low, about 300 m, but at 38 to 39 degrees south, cooled by latitude and strong winds. The wind keeps grapes healthy and thickens skins. Pinot Noir, Malbec and Merlot make fresher, more elegant wines than in Mendoza. Some Río Negro vines date from the early 20th century.
What keeps Patagonia cool, compared with Salta?
Patagonia is low, so its coolness comes from latitude and constant wind.
The same grape, Malbec, from Salta, Mendoza and Patagonia makes a great tasting lesson. Altitude, latitude and wind each leave a mark.
Which statements about Salta are true?
Mendoza is by far Argentina's largest region.
Salta has vineyards up to 3,000 m and floral Torrontés
Patagonia is cooled by latitude and wind
Argentina's styles vary with altitude and latitude
Compare them with the Andean countries

Uruguay has a humid, maritime climate influenced by the Atlantic and the Río de la Plata. Tannat, brought by Basque immigrants in the 1870s, is its national grape, giving dark, tannic reds that are often softer than in France's Madiran. Canelones, near Montevideo, is the main region; Maldonado, on the coast, makes fresh whites like Albariño.

Brazil's main region is Serra Gaúcha, in the far south, settled by Italian immigrants. It's wet and humid, which suits early-picked grapes for sparkling wine, now Brazil's strength. Vale dos Vinhedos was its first GI. In the north-east, the São Francisco Valley, near the equator, harvests twice a year with irrigation.
Why is sparkling wine well suited to Serra Gaúcha?
Its humid climate suits early-picked, high-acid grapes
It has very hot, dry summers
Rain and humidity make full ripeness hard; early picking for sparkling wine keeps acidity and avoids rot.

Unlike Chile and Argentina, Uruguay and southern Brazil have rain in the growing season, more like Bordeaux than Mendoza. Growers fight disease rather than drought. Their wines tend to be lower in alcohol and fresher, a counterpoint to the ripe, sunny Andean style.
Yes. Basque immigrants brought it in the 1870s, and it covers about a quarter of the vineyards.
Uruguay's humid climate gives Tannat a softer style
Brazil's strength is sparkling wine from Serra Gaúcha
The Atlantic side fights rain, not drought
